1:
The cave is located and then measured. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) puts it in a tributary ravine of the valley of Elah, the highway from Philistia to Hebron, where many natural caves, roomy and dry, are still used by shepherds as dwellings and refuges for their flocks. The name he derives from the old Canaanitish city of Adullam, whose ruins are still visible on a hill to the south. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) does not ask whether the fastness was natural or artificial, only that its access was so difficult that David thought himself able, with Goliath’s sword, to keep it against all Saul’s forces, and so buried himself alive in it, among those the apostle describes as wandering in dens and caves of the earth.

What sort of men gathered there is the real dispute. Henry is unsparing: the regiment was made up not of great men, nor rich, nor stout, no, nor good men, but men in distress, in debt and discontented, men of broken fortunes and restless spirits: see what weak instruments God uses. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) contests this directly. It is possible, he grants, that such men first supposed David would be glad of help in revenging himself, and might profit by plunder; but if so they were disappointed, for they are never found plundering or murdering, always appear under good discipline, and are employed only in beneficent service and their country’s defence, David having civilised them and made profitable to the state those who were unprofitable. It is not necessary, he adds pointedly, to strain the original to prove them exceptionable characters, as some have done. Ellicott sides with him, citing Ewald: the melancholy state of the country under Saul drove men to seek a leader, many of the refugees were prominent Israelites, and David organised them into a force which guarded the exposed southern frontier and won a popularity that served him well later.

Moab is explained by kinship, geography and politics. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) read Mizpeh as literally a watch-tower, here a proper name for a mountain fastness on the high land bounding the plains of Moab east of the Dead Sea, most likely in the mountains of Abarim, reached from Bethlehem by crossing Jordan near its mouth. Ellicott notes this Mizpeh is named nowhere else, and grounds the visit in blood, Jesse being Ruth the Moabitess’s grandson. John Gill (reformed) says the name distinguishes it from the place so called in Israel, that Junius makes it a fortified place, and that David might think himself safer there, in an enemy’s land, than at home. Clarke adds that the king of Moab, an enemy of Saul, would be the readier to oblige a man from whom he might expect friendship. Henry keeps to the son: the first thing David does is find his aged parents a quiet habitation, whatever became of himself.

Ellicott makes one observation no one else touches. Addressing the Moabite king, David speaks of God and not of Jehovah, which Ellicott takes for reverence, an idolater having nothing to do with the name by which the Eternal was known to his covenant people; yet the Name was not unknown in Moab, its letters standing in Mesha’s inscription. On the hold he and John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) part: Ellicott takes it for one place, the hold from which Gad orders David away and most likely in Moab, while Wesley reads a singular put for a plural, holds in general, for as long as David had to move from place to place. Why Gad sent him back divides them too: Henry makes it the confidence of a man assured of his innocency and of the divine protection and desirous to serve his tribe, Wesley that he should publicly claim the kingdom after Saul’s death, so his friends might appear for him.
6:
The council is staged with care, the spear read as an emblem. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) corrects the setting to its literal sense, Saul abiding in Gibeah, his own royal city, under the tamarisk tree upon the height; his love of trees has been noticed before, and the darkest deed of his reign was settled in the spot he loved best. He finds here one of the earliest councils of which we have any definite account: the king leaning on his spear, surrounded by captains of his own tribe save one, the Edomite over the royal herds. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) reads the spear as the ensign of power, stuck in the ground where the king rested, marking for the soldiers their general’s tent. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) makes the spear a sceptre, intimating the force by which Saul designed to rule.

Two voices hear the appeal to tribe as self-incriminating. Ellicott calls it a fair specimen of Saul’s later rule, and no wonder the people were estranged from one of whom they had once been proud: we have it from his own mouth that he had given all the posts of honour to men of his own tribe and family, or to strangers like the Edomite, so his argument amounts to asking who but a Benjamite would honour only Benjamites. Such a sovereign, he says, had forfeited his kingdom, and the consequence was the thin array he could muster in his need on the fatal field of Gilboa. Henry turns the words into three charges: that they were unwise, since David advanced would carry into Judah the honour now in Benjamin and would have no such fields and vineyards to reward them with; that they were unfaithful; and that they were unkind, none of them being sorry for him.

How much Saul knew of the covenant is left open. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) allow both readings: he may have heard something of what passed between Jonathan and David, or may merely mean the friendship well known to him. Ellicott comes down on the first, the terms being too pointed for the old friendship alone, so that Saul had learned something of the farewell interview at the New Moon feast. Of the complaint that no one was sorry for him he says only that it is strangely real and pathetic. John Gill (reformed) explains how the charge arose: they had not revolted nor committed any overt act, but because they did not disclose what he supposed they knew, he read their silence as treason. Henry calls it jealous malice, with its pitiful arts to extort discoveries of things that are not.

Whether Doeg told the truth about the inquiry divides four ways. Clarke thinks the circumstance, though not in the earlier history, probably true, since David would naturally wish to know where to direct his steps in such a crisis. Keil and Delitzsch agree it took place, their ground being that Ahimelech never disclaims it when challenged. Ellicott holds it by no means certain: nothing was said of the Urim and Thummim being brought out at David’s visit, and Doeg may have been misled by seeing the high priest enter the sanctuary, where the ephod stood and behind it the sword, to fetch it. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) calls it a lie, David charging the man with lying in a psalm, and thinks he told many lies not here expressed, besides concealing what he was bound to declare for Ahimelech’s defence. Gill reports the suspicion but will not hold it, and adds what no one else notices: by the Jewish writers the inquiry was itself the treason charged, since inquiry by Urim was not made for a private person but for a king, so that to say Ahimelech inquired was to say David had made himself king and the priest owned him.
11:
That the whole priestly house was summoned, and not the one man accused, is read as evidence of intent. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) says this sending for them all to Gibeah, when Ahimelech alone was to blame if blame there was, looks as though Saul and Doeg had already determined upon the wholesale massacre that followed. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) supplies a different frame, that these were the priests of the house of Eli, which God had threatened to cut off. John Gill (reformed) notes the contempt in the arraignment itself: Saul does not so much as call the man by his name, nor give him the title of his office, though he was the second person in the kingdom, and to whose office the civil government had been annexed a few years before.

Ahimelech’s answer is weighed for what it does and does not concede. Ellicott calls his words quiet and dignified, and takes them to speak the general sentiment of the people about David: what the guardian of the sanctuary had done he had done as a matter of course for one so closely related to the king, and one who had always proved loyal and devoted. Wesley reads the same speech more narrowly, that the high priest does not determine the quarrel between Saul and David, nor affirm what David now was, but only declares what David formerly had been and what he was still for anything he knew to the contrary. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) raises a lexical possibility that would change the sentence altogether, that the word translated faithful is probably the name of an office.

The one charge Ahimelech troubles to answer is the inquiry, and how his answer is rendered decides whether there was treason at all. Ellicott observes that the consultation of the Urim for David is the charge Saul repeats and the only one the priest takes up, and he prefers the rendering Abarbanel gives in Lange: that was the first day that I enquired of God for him, and I did not know that it was displeasing to thee. Gill reports the same alternative from Kimchi, read without the interrogation, though his own sense is the opposite, that this was far from the first time, David having often consulted the Lord through him when going upon the king’s business, and always as innocently and as much for the king’s service as now. Clarke takes it the same way, that the inquiry was no new thing and he had never been told it was either wrong in itself or displeasing to the king, nor is it likely he knew of any disagreement, since he knew David only as the king’s son-in-law and treated him as such.

What hangs on the rendering, Ellicott alone spells out. If the received translation stands, the only possible explanation is that David had been in the habit of consulting the Urim on special occasions for the king; and the right to consult it, when there was a king in Israel, belonged to the king alone. He cites the Talmud as authoritative on this point, that the king, or the chief of the legislative administration, who alone had that privilege, stood facing the priest while the priest faced the ineffable name deposited with the Urim within the breastplate. On the sentence itself two voices are brief and both are damning. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) say that notwithstanding this truthful assertion of his innocence Saul pronounced sentence of death, and not upon the high priest only. Gill adds that he pronounced it himself, without taking the opinion or advice of others and without further time, an act of arbitrary power upon an innocent person and of great injustice.
17:
The guards who refused are identified, then commended. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) renders the word literally as runners, guards or lictors who ran by the royal chariot as an escort, still the usual attendants of any great man in the East, a service Samuel had warned the people their king would require. Their refusal he endorses through Wordsworth: they were more faithful in disobeying than if they had obeyed an order against the commandment of the Lord, whose servant the king was no less than they. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) says they dared to disobey in a case of such injustice, inhumanity and irreligion. John Gill (reformed) reports the Jewish tradition that these runners were Abner and Amasa, but gives Kimchi’s objection that those two were no footmen but princes and captains.

Why the work fell to the Edomite is answered practically and nationally. Gill puts it bluntly: Saul was determined they should die, and if one would not do it another should, and who so fit for this bloody work as their false accuser and false witness? John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) reads the naming of his race as deliberate, set down to wipe the stain of the butchery off the Israelite nation and to show why he was so ready for it, being of a people that bore implacable hatred against Israel and the priests of the Lord. Ellicott supposes he was helped by his own servants, and reports that for this act he has been execrated in the most ancient Jewish writings above perhaps any other wicked man of Scripture: the Babylonian Talmud tells how three destructive demons met him afterwards, one taking his learning, one burning his soul, one scattering his dust in the synagogues.

The number of the dead and the dress they died in are both pressed. Clarke notes the Septuagint reads three hundred and five men and Josephus three hundred and eighty-five, and suggests the eighty-five were the priests and the three hundred their families, all Nob’s population; the linen ephod, he adds, marks those who administered, or had the right to administer, in sacred things. Ellicott takes the garment to be a linen over-vestment worn by the ordinary priests, similar to the high priestly cape, and thinks they had come from Nob to Gibeah in official costume out of respect to the king who sent for them, so the deed assumes a still more awful character when we recollect who the victims were, clad in their white ministering robes. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) make the point grammatically, that the allusion to the priestly clothing, like the repeated phrase priests of Jehovah, shows the crime in its true light, since the very dress they wore as consecrated servants ought to have made their murderers shrink.

On the destruction of the city the voices compete in condemnation, and one locates the real blasphemy. Keil and Delitzsch observe that Saul, not content even with this, had the whole town destroyed as a city laid under the ban, so completely identifying his private revenge with the cause of Jehovah that he avenged a supposed conspiracy against his own person as treason against Jehovah the God-king. Clarke calls it one of the worst acts of Saul’s life, his malice implacable and his wrath cruel, with no motive of justice or policy by which such barbarity can be justified. Wesley goes further: in all Saul’s life there is no wickedness to be compared with it, he appears now wholly under the power of the evil spirit which had long tormented him, and the destruction could not but go to the heart of every pious Israelite and make them wish a thousand times they had been content with Samuel’s government. Gill will not settle whose hand it was, Doeg’s or Saul’s, noting Josephus has the king send men to slay all the inhabitants.
20:
How the one priest came to be alive is answered the same way thrice. John Gill (reformed) supposes Abiathar was left by his father to care for the sanctuary and its holy things when the rest were summoned, and that on hearing of the execution he took the ephod, with the Urim and Thummim, and escaped before the king’s messengers could reach Nob. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) gives the same suggestion, that he remained behind to perform the necessary functions there and fled on hearing of the death of his father and his brother priests. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) adds that he had intelligence of the danger in time to shift for his own safety, and asks where else he should go but to David. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) confirms Gill’s detail from a later chapter, that the man carried his sacerdotal garments with him.

Ellicott alone disturbs the sequence the chapter seems to give. The exact period of Abiathar’s coming to the exiled band is uncertain, he says, since in many of the recitals in this book no note of time is given; it is therefore probable that the meeting with David did not take place immediately after the massacre, nor even directly after the destruction of Nob, and from a statement in the following chapter it would appear he only joined David at Keilah. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) keep to the plain reading, that he fled after David, that is to David the fugitive, and told him of the barbarous vengeance Saul had taken on the priests of the Lord.

How far David was to blame is the one place these voices will not agree. Clarke makes him guiltless: seeing the Edomite there he suspected he would make the matter known, and he has been the innocent cause of their destruction. Henry will not have it so mild. David lamented the calamity, he says, but especially his being accessory to it, and must have been much pained to consider that his own falsehood was one cause of this fatal event; indeed he knew the man’s character so well that he feared some such mischief when he saw him at the sanctuary. Henry notes too that David calls him the Edomite because he kept the heart of an Edomite, though by embracing the Jewish religion he had put on the mask of an Israelite. Keil and Delitzsch settle the lexical question under the dispute, that the verb David uses carries the sense of being the cause of a thing, a meaning the root has in Arabic and Talmudic usage.

The promise of protection is read as a legal word and as an obligation. Keil and Delitzsch note that the noun rendered safeguard is an abstract, protection or keeping, used here for the concrete, so the sense is simply: thou art protected with me. Clarke draws out what it cost: Saul’s enmity is directed against Abiathar as well as David, so he can have no safety but in being closely attached to him, and David undertakes to defend him even at the risk of his own life, which he was bound in duty and conscience to do. Gill observes the man plainly appeared to be in a fright, not knowing what to do nor where to go. Henry closes on the symmetry of it: David had now not only a prophet with him but a priest, and a high priest, which was a happy omen of his success, and yet Saul also had a high priest, since he had a Urim to consult, for even those who hate the power of godliness will not be without the form. Ellicott adds from the Talmudic tradition that the Edomite had been brought up with Saul in the family of Kish, and was jealous for his master with the passionate jealousy often found in old servants.
